2026 U.S. House

Where your House candidates stand on AI data centers

Every district on the 2026 ballot — 440 of them, 1161 candidates — and what each one has actually said or done about data centers, with the link behind it. Your representative votes on the federal rules; your county votes on the project. This is the federal half.

440districts on the ballot1161candidates filed100with a documented record272on the record only for the 417-3 vote48unverified mentions queued

The election was 20 days ago. Results are recorded for 434 of 440 races, each linked to the page it was read from; 6 more are in a runoff or not yet called. 78 of the winners have a documented data-center record here. This page is now an archive: what each representative promised about data centers while asking for the job. Hold the winners to it — and see the officials scorecard for what they have actually done since.

Coverage here is very low, and saying so is the point. 100 of 1161 candidates have a documented data-center record. Another 272 are on the record only for voting yes when the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3 (roll call 312). That vote is listed on their records but labelled Consensus vote only and never scored, because a vote nearly every member cast says little about any one of them. The rest show no record found — never "neutral". At 440 districts this page starts as a complete ballot and an almost-empty record; it fills in as scan_candidate_records.py surfaces leads and a human verifies them. How that works.

AK-AL

Alaska · PVI R+6 · Nick Begich III (Republican) · Incumbent advanced to general

Result: Nick Begich III (Republican) won. Called. — source, read 2026-11-21.

At stake in this state: 5 data centers · 0.1 TWh/year · 2 local moratoriums in force

Nick Begich III (Republican) · incumbent Won Mixed

Introduced the DATA Act of 2026 to let energy-intensive users, which he says include data centers, run on self-contained 'grid of one' power so ratepayers do not subsidize new load, and argued in an op-ed that Alaska should use its energy advantage to attract AI investment and not 'regulate too early.'

  • Introduced the DATA Act of 2026 with Reps. Crenshaw and Owens; the release says it lets manufacturers and other energy-intensive industries run fully isolated off-grid power so 'innovation can scale without forcing households to subsidize massive new energy demands.' (2026-04-21 — source)
  • Op-ed: said Alaska's natural gas, renewables and stranded energy assets are an advantage for AI data centers; said the DATA Act protects ratepayers from subsidizing new loads; wrote 'We can hesitate, regulate too early and risk becoming an observer... or we can engage thoughtfully, strategically and on our own terms.' (2026-04-23 — source)
  • Voted yes on H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed 417-3 (roll call 312). It directs state utility commissions to consider rate designs making data centers with 100 MW or more of peak demand at one site pay the full incremental cost of the generation and grid upgrades they require. A near-unanimous vote: shown on the record, not scored on its own. (2026-09-16 — source)

Record read 2026-11-21.

Introduced the SHIELD Act with Rep. Kathy Castor (separate rate class for large-load customers over 75 MW), co-led the Energy Bills Relief Act, and is a cosponsor of the Responsible Data Center Siting Act.

  • Introduced, with Rep. Kathy Castor, the Stopping Hikes In Electricity from Large Load Demands (SHIELD) Act: a separate rate class for large load customers (facilities using more than 75MW) so households do not pay for their grid upgrades, plus priority interconnection for large loads powered by zero-emission electricity. "Families should not be forced to subsidize massive energy costs for billion-dollar companies." (2026-01-14 — source)
  • With Rep. Sean Casten, led 120 House Democrats in introducing the Energy Bills Relief Act, which Levin said "ensures that data centers and large energy users pay their fair share instead of passing those costs onto families and small businesses." (2026-03-18 — source)
  • Listed as a cosponsor of H.R. 10321, the Responsible Data Center Siting Act of 2026 (sponsor Rep. Suhas Subramanyam), 'to direct the Secretary of Energy to establish best practices for the siting of data centers'. (2026-09-08 — source)

  • Introduced H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, with Rep. Kathy Castor. Suhas Subramanyam (Democratic) · incumbent Won Guardrails

Represents a district with more than 300 data centers; introduced a DHS security-strategy bill for communities around data centers (May 2026) and, with Reps. Obernolte and Foushee, a bipartisan NIST/DOE data center energy and water measurement bill (June 2026); sponsor of H.R. 10321, the Responsible Data Center Siting Act. At a Brookings event said he wants a national strategy that puts communities first.

  • Introduced the Data Infrastructure Risk Reduction Act, directing DHS to produce a security strategy and recommendations for protecting communities around data centers, considering the security of transmission and water infrastructure. (2026-05-08 — source)
  • Introduced, with Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Valerie Foushee (D-NC), the Data Infrastructure Energy Measurement and Standards Act, directing NIST in coordination with DOE to develop best practices and technical standards for measuring data center energy and water use, as a foundation for forecasting, planning and siting. "We need a simple way to track how much power and water these facilities use." (2026-06-18 — source)
  • At a Brookings Institution event called the community-by-community approach to data center siting "short-term profit-driven, sometimes it's a little predatory, and it's not working" and said he wants "a national strategy that puts communities first"; also called for transparency in development agreements, which often include nondisclosure agreements signed by officials, and on actual power and water use. (2026-09-22 — source)
  • Voted yes on H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed 417-3 (roll call 312). It directs state utility commissions to consider rate designs making data centers with 100 MW or more of peak demand at one site pay the full incremental cost of the generation and grid upgrades they require. A near-unanimous vote: shown on the record, not scored on its own. (2026-09-16 — source)

How this page is built, and how it stays current

The ballot is primary-sourced. Every district links the state election authority's own certified candidate list. 435 voting districts plus 5 non-voting delegates, and where mid-decade redistricting put two sitting members in one seat, both are shown.

Every claim carries its own link and date, and a record older than 120 days is flagged as needing a re-read rather than shown as current.

Silence is disclosed, never scored. “Lean” summarises only the cited items below it, on one axis: does this candidate's documented position make data centers pay their own way and give the host community a say? It is not an overall rating, not a grade, and not an endorsement. Candidates with no located record are left unscored.

Records are promoted by a human, never by a script. scripts/scan_candidate_records.py mines the news archive for a candidate's name alongside data-center terms and files what it finds into data/candidate_record_candidates.json. It never writes this registry — promotion is where source and as_of come from, and those are the two fields that make a claim quotable at a hearing. scripts/verify_candidate_records.py then re-checks every published link and flags what has gone stale or dead.

“Recent mentions” are not records. Where a card shows them, they are unreviewed headlines matched by script — the same bargain the story tracker already makes. They are leads for the queue, and the page says so on every block.

Lean labels

  • Guardrails — Documented support for making data centers carry their own costs, for community say over siting, or for a pause.
  • Mixed — Documented on both sides — courts the buildout but backs some ratepayer or community protection.
  • Accelerate — Documented emphasis on building faster — competitiveness, incentives, or siting help — without a matching cost or community safeguard on the record.
  • Consensus vote only — On the record only for a near-unanimous vote (the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3). Shown, not scored — a vote nearly everyone cast says little about any one member.
  • No record found — No documented statement or action on data centers located. Not scored — the gap is disclosed, not punished.

Found something we missed?

A statement, a bill, a vote, a local story — send the link and we will read it. Contact.

As of August 2026 (3m ago) · changes weekly — re-check before citing

The ballot is complete and primary-sourced — 435 voting districts plus 5 delegates, each read from the state election authority's certified candidate list. The AI/data-center records are the opposite: almost every candidate has none located, and renders as no record found rather than as neutral. Treat a blank as 'nobody has checked', not as 'nothing to find'. Rosters also move — pending primaries, withdrawals and redistricting litigation all change the field, so check the linked state list before quoting a name.
